description: We are a team of students studying Software Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, and Aerospace Engineering, brought together by an unexpected common interest: shabushabu. What started as a shared love for food eventually led us to join the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. With our diverse academic backgrounds, we developed HoneyMoon, a web-based platform that helps identify suitable landing sites near the Moon’s south pole.
summary:
HoneyMoon is a web tool that ranks landing sites at the lunar south pole and shows the best arrival day for each. The user enters the trip purpose, arrival date, length of stay, crewed or robotic mission, power and communication needs, and an optional slope limit. The backend checks 72,297 sites hour by hour for the whole stay. It combines JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions for 2026–2028 with an 80 m LOLA terrain model, which gives each site’s skyline in 720 directions out to 100 km. Sites are scored on communication, flatness, roughness, sunlight and the mission objective (shadowed regions, geology, craters). Each result comes with a skyline chart, an hourly timeline and a score breakdown.

At the south pole, lighting at a given site shifts by two to three weeks from one year to the next, so last year’s good dates may not work. HoneyMoon lets mission planners, lander teams and students see these trade-offs in one search. Our long-term sunlight and Earth-view results match NASA’s average maps, with correlations of 0.984 and 0.980 across 2,000 sites.
details:
What it does and how it works

HoneyMoon helps a user decide where and when to land at the lunar south pole. The user sets the landing date, length of stay, crewed or robotic mission, science objective, power and communication needs, an optional slope limit, and importance weights from 1 to 5. The backend scores 72,297 grid sites (1 km spacing, south of 85°S) on communication, flatness, roughness, sunlight and the mission objective, and returns ranked sites with the best arrival day within a search window of up to 30 days. On the map, zooming and panning refresh the recommendations for the visible area on a finer grid. Each site has a score breakdown with exclusion reasons, a 3D terrain view built from the elevation model, and an hourly Sun and Earth timeline.

The terrain is processed once: from the 80 m LOLA elevation model we trace each site’s skyline in 720 directions out to 100 km, for observer heights of 1, 5 and 10 m. Each search then checks only the hours of the stay against an hourly JPL Horizons table of Sun and Earth positions (2026–2028, 26,304 entries). Mission objectives are defined based on the NASA Artemis III Science Definition Team Report, considering shadowed regions, geological units within 20 km, and craters with diameters of 20 km or more.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission planners can compare sites and dates in one search. Robotic lander teams can size batteries and radio plans around dark and no-signal hours. Students can explore why the south pole is hard to land on.

Validation and limits

At 2,000 sites, our Sun and Earth visibility matches NASA’s average maps with correlations of 0.984 and 0.980. Our 80 m skyline stays within about 1.3° of 5 m terrain in 95% of directions (100 sites, 1 m height). A cross-check with LROC stereo terrain gave about 1.5°, so the Earth visibility margin (0.25°) is labeled provisional.

Tools

Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, Numba, GeoPandas, Shapely, PyProj, PostgreSQL, Docker, Railway. Frontend: React 19, Vite 8, Three.js, NASA Moon Trek tiles, LROC WAC imagery, Vercel. Data: NASA PGDA (LOLA), JPL Horizons, USGS geologic map and crater database, MIT illumination maps. Claude was used for analysis and design drafts.

GitHub: https://github.com/ShabuShabu2026

What is creative

The interface works like a flight search: simple by default, with advanced settings (slope limit, visibility criteria, observer height) when needed. Scores include the longest dark period and the longest communication blackout, so one three-day outage ranks below three short ones.

What we considered

Lighting at a site shifts by two to three weeks between years, so we check every hour of the planned stay. We kept crewed and uncrewed constraints separate and made the 5° slope limit adjustable. We also stated the 80 m terrain resolution, the Earth margin and the sample sizes in the results.
